title: Trades With a Fee Each Time
statement:
You get prices, where prices[i] is a share's price on day i, and a broker fee. You may make as many trades as you like, but you can hold at most one share at a time, so you must sell before buying again.

Every completed trade (one buy followed by one sell) costs fee once. Return the largest total profit you can make. Doing nothing gives 0.

examples.why: Buy at 2, sell at 6 (gain 2 after the fee), buy at 3, sell at 9 (gain 4). One long trade from 2 to 9 earns only 5.
Here the small dip is not worth a second fee: two trades give 1 + 1, while holding from 2 to 9 gives 7 − 3 = 4.
Prices only fall, so the best plan is not to trade.

hints: At the end of any day you are in one of two situations: holding a share or not. What is the best profit you can have in each?
Let cash be the best profit while holding nothing and hold the best profit while holding one share. Each day, each can come from staying put or from one trade action.
cash = max(cash, hold + price − fee), hold = max(hold, cash − price). Charging the fee on the sell is enough, since each trade has exactly one sell.

explain.intuition:
Summing every price rise, the trick that works without fees, breaks here: each rise you trade separately costs another fee, so small dips are often better ridden out. What you need is a way to compare "sell now" with "keep holding" without guessing the future.

Track two numbers as the days go by: cash, the best profit if you hold nothing tonight, and hold, the best profit if you own a share tonight (it is negative after a purchase, since you spent money). Each day, cash either stays or comes from selling today, and hold either stays or comes from buying today. These two states are a tiny state machine, and every possible trading plan is one path through it.
steps: For each later day with price p: newCash = max(cash, hold + p − fee).
Assign both and continue. Return cash, since ending with a share never helps.
pitfalls: Adding every positive day-to-day change and subtracting a fee for each. Example 2 pays the fee twice where once is better.
Charging the fee on both the buy and the sell. It is once per completed trade.
Updating hold with today's new cash. That allows selling and rebuying on the same day; here it happens to be harmless, but in the cooldown variant the same habit gives wrong answers.

solutions.title: Try every buy day for every sell day
solutions.idea: best[j] is the best profit by day j with nothing held. Either do nothing on day j, or sell on day j a share bought on some earlier day i, on top of best[i].

solutions.title: Two states: cash and hold
solutions.idea: Keep the best profit while holding nothing and while holding a share. Each day, each state either stays or switches by one buy or sell.

followups: After a sale you must wait one day before buying again. Which state do you add?
You may complete at most k trades. How do the states change, and what does that cost?
